I'm a 49-year-old farmer in Quzhou County. I've been farming this land for nearly 30 years, since I left middle school and came back to help my father. My family has about 12 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know every plot like the back of my hand.

This year, I'm sticking with what I know works. I'll put 10 mu into wheat-maize double cropping and keep 2 mu in cotton. The wheat-maize rotation is our bread and butter — the county extension agent says it's the most efficient system for our soil, and my neighbor Lao Zhang got over 500 kg per mu on his wheat last year doing the same thing. Cotton prices have been up and down, but 2 mu is manageable for my wife and me to handle, and it gives us some cash flow in the autumn when the grain prices are still uncertain.

For wheat, I'll plant an improved variety around October 10th. I usually buy my wheat seed from the township supply store — it's not the most expensive hybrid, but it's reliable and I save some seed from the year before to mix in. I'll rotary till the land before planting to break up the corn stubble. Fertilizer-wise, the extension guy told me 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I always go a bit more because I'd rather waste a little money than risk a bad harvest. I'll put down compound fertilizer as base — about 18 kg nitrogen, 13 kg phosphate, and 5 kg potassium per mu — and topdress once at jointing if the wheat looks yellow. I'll irrigate four times: winter irrigation, then at jointing, heading, and grain filling. Water costs keep going up, but you can't skip irrigation on the North China Plain. For pests, I'll spray herbicide once after planting and maybe insecticide twice if I see aphids.

For summer maize, I'll plant a hybrid variety — probably Nongda or Denghai, whatever the dealer has in stock — right after wheat harvest in early June. The window is tight, maybe five days, so I'll use no-tillage planting to save time. Maize is hungrier than wheat; I'll give it about 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphate, and 4 kg potassium per mu, all as compound fertilizer at planting. If it doesn't rain for two weeks in July, I'll irrigate twice. Maize usually needs 2 or 3 pesticide sprays — herbicide at planting, and insecticide for armyworms if they show up.

The cotton goes in around April 20th. I'll rotary till that plot and plant a hybrid cotton variety. Cotton needs more fertilizer than people think — I'll use about 20 kg nitrogen, 10 kg phosphate, and 6 kg potassium per mu, split between basal and topdressing at flowering. I'll irrigate twice and spray pesticide about 10 times because bollworms and aphids never leave cotton alone. It's labor-intensive, but the 2 mu is worth it.

I expect about 480 kg per mu for wheat, 520 kg per mu for maize, and around 380 kg per mu of seed cotton. These are reasonable numbers if the weather cooperates — not great years, not drought years, just normal.
